items.title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.desc: The "Into the Unknown" benchmark tasks nine AI agents with tackling open research questions from U.S. national laboratories. None of the 135 submissions meets all requirements. A total of 114 papers fail the integrity check, with agents claiming to have conducted experiments that never took place. GPT-6 Astra performs best but still doesn't meet the experts' standards. The article Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened. Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out. According to the paper , none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all. A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards. Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet. Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet. The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours. Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation. The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro , Kimi K3 , and GLM-5.3 . Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3. items.title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.desc: Google Research built an AI that spots signs of high blood pressure using only the pulse and motion sensors in a standard smartwatch, no cuff needed. In a 196-person study, its 65.8 percent detection rate beat the traditional in-office measurement. The method is already live in the Google Health app, though it doesn't replace a formal diagnosis. The article Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post . The study was published in Nature . A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data. In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement. Ad Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google. items.title: Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model
items.desc: Ricursive Intelligence is releasing Ripple-65B Preview, a 65-billion-parameter open-weight language model that the company says achieves the top score among open-source U.S. models on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark at a total R&D cost of $32 million. On other benchmarks, however, Ripple falls behind the likewise newly released western open model Inkling 2 Small. The article Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI chip design firm Ricursive Intelligence has trained an open language model. Ripple-65B Preview was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens and, according to the company, achieved a score of 80.52 on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark, the best result among open US models. Ripple partly uses Terminus 2 and partly OpenCode as its harness. Other benchmark results show that Ripple does not match the also newly released Inkling 2 Small , but Ripple is likely easier to deploy on users' own hardware. According to Ricursive, total development and training costs amounted to just $32 million, covering all research and development expenses. The model uses a dense Transformer architecture with 65 billion parameters instead of the more common mixture-of-experts approach and is optimized for Nvidia hardware. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. items.desc: Perplexity is launching "Teammates," always-on agents that work through ongoing projects on their own virtual machines. The feature requires the Max plan at $200 per month, well above similar offerings from OpenAI or Anthropic. The market for always-on agents is getting crowded. items.full: Perplexity now has its own AI agent that runs around the clock and handles work tasks on its own. While Perplexity Computer executes one-off assignments, the new Teammates stay active and work through ongoing projects independently. Each Teammate runs on its own virtual machine with a desktop and browser. Users track progress through dedicated threads in the Perplexity app and can interact with the agents via Slack. Perplexity joins SpaceX, Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, which already offer similar agents through Grok Bots, Muse , Dots , and Duet . Teammates require the Max plan at $200 per month. Dots start at $100, and Duet is available from $20. In practice, the cheaper options will likely hit their usage limits fast. Just days ago, high agent consumption forced SpaceX to impose stricter usage caps on Grok Bots . Perplexity's annualized revenue topped $750 million as of August. items.full: Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 6, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins. Six times a year, THE DECODER's editorial team takes a deep dive into a foundational AI topic in its "Frontier Radar" series, published as a newsletter and exclusively on the site for THE DECODER subscribers . Issue #5 profiles 27 AI labs in detail, sorted by six research bets, plus nearly 20 more in brief and an overview covering origins, valuations, and what's publicly available. Issue #1 covered the current state of agentic AI. Issue #2 examined the measurable impact of AI on productivity. Issue #3 covered the emerging token economy of generative AI. Issue #4 asked what's left of the AI lead over China and where Europe stands. After the launch of GPT-6 Astra, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X: "AGI has arrived." OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the model a turning point and welcomed humanity to the "AGI era" . What exactly the two men mean isn't clear, since there's no agreed-upon definition of AGI. The message comes through anyway: an extremely powerful AI, possibly a self-improving one, is imminent and the path is mapped out. Many of the people who built today's systems apparently see things differently. Dozens have left the big labs to start their own. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist; now he's building Safe Superintelligence . Jerry Tworek led the development of OpenAI's reasoning models and now runs Core Automation . David Silver, the mind behind AlphaGo, left Google DeepMind for Ineffable Intelligence . Yann LeCun left Meta after twelve years and founded AMI . Jeff Dean spent 27 years at Google, most recently as chief scientist, and started Discovery Loop . The money follows: Nvidia invested in SSI in July, reportedly five billion dollars according to Bloomberg. The lab hasn't released a single model or paper. Prometheus, Jeff Bezos' industrial AI lab, pulled in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June. Flapping Airplanes has no public model either and raised one billion dollars in an October Series A. The motives are mixed, and not all technical. At these valuations, founders become paper billionaires fast. LeCun left after a strategy dispute with Meta . Sutskever wants to do research without product pressure . Others want to carve out a niche that would be a sideshow at a big lab. Some departures aren't even a clean break: Google itself is a founding investor in Discovery Loop. items.title: The Essential Guide to Proxy Services, Locations, and IP Types
items.desc: Pick a proxy by matching three things: what you are doing, where the IP should appear, and what type of IP you need. A proxy is just a middle stop between you and a website. It hides your real IP and shows another one instead. This matters because IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion possible […]
items.full: Facebook Tweet Pin LinkedIn Pick a proxy by matching three things: what you are doing, where the IP should appear, and what type of IP you need. A proxy is just a middle stop between you and a website. It hides your real IP and shows another one instead. This matters because IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion possible addresses, so clean IPs are limited and valuable [source: ARIN] . TLDR: Use datacenter proxies for speed, residential proxies for trust, and mobile proxies for app-like traffic. Choose the location closest to your target market, such as a US proxy for checking US prices. For example, a retailer testing 500 product pages from 5 countries may use rotating residential proxies to reduce blocks by 30% or more. Do not buy the biggest plan first. Test a small batch. A proxy is like a friendly stunt double for your internet connection. You send a request. The proxy sends it forward. The website sees the proxy IP, not yours. This is useful for many normal tasks. Price tracking. Ad checks. SEO tools. Market research. Social media management. Website testing. Even checking if your site loads correctly in another country. It is not magic, though. Bad proxies get blocked. Slow proxies waste your day. Honestly, it feels like some proxy dashboards were built to make you click seven times just to change one setting. Nobody needs that. Proxy services usually fall into a few buckets. Each one has a job. Location can change everything. A website may show different prices in New York, London, and Berlin. Search results also change by country and city. Ads do too. If you run local SEO checks, use city-level proxies. If you test global pricing, use country-level proxies. If you watch how an app behaves on a mobile network, use mobile proxies from that carrier region. Expect to waste time on weak location filters. Some tools say “US” but give you random states. That can add 10 to 20 seconds per check when you need exact local results. Annoying? Very. There are also different ways proxies can behave. This part matters a lot. For example, use rotating residential proxies when checking thousands of product pages. Use sticky residential proxies when you need to stay logged in for 10 minutes. Use dedicated datacenter proxies when speed matters more than looking human. Start with the task. Do not start with the price page. That is how people end up buying the wrong plan. Also check the provider’s uptime. Many aim for 99% or higher. That sounds nice, but test it yourself. One hour of downtime during a launch can hurt. Some proxy deals look great. Then the pain starts. A good proxy provider should show speed, success rate, location options, and traffic limits. You should also get simple docs. If setup takes an hour for a basic username and password, something is wrong. Proxy services are simple once you split them into three parts: service type, location, and IP behavior . Match those to your task. Test before you scale. Keep records of blocks, speed, and success rates. Your best proxy is not the fanciest one. It is the one that gets the job done without making you mutter at your screen.

items.title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
items.desc: AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs, according to a study by Anthropic researcher Andy Hall. GPT-5 found about 98 percent of reward-hacking cases, but the more exhaustively the search is tuned, the more false alarms pile up. That's not yet enough for reliable safety checks. The article AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds Manuel Uth Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious. That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident. In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views. Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR . METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half. In sandbagging , a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs. Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did. Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug. Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs. GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either. items.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
items.desc: Thinking Machines' AI model Inkling 2 Small swears during its internal reasoning, 316 times across 2,655 benchmark runs, according to an analysis by Vals AI. The profanity typically shows up late in long runs that fail anyway. But it doesn't work as a warning signal: 96 percent of failed runs contained no cursing at all. The article Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its internal chain of thought. Researchers at Vals AI read the model's thinking logs from 2,655 runs across 13 benchmarks and found "fuck" or variations in 50 runs, totaling 316 instances. 241 came from just two runs that spiraled out of control. In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. ProgramBench was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected. Inkling 2 Small typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter.
